ideas.title: Your knuckle crack is a bubble, not your bones
ideas.angle: Bust the 'bones grinding' myth: an MRI showed a gas cavity forming; scientists still argue about collapse; and no, it does not cause arthritis.

ideas.title: The man who cracked one hand for 60 years
Why you can't crack the same knuckle twice
ideas.angle: Explain the bubble that stays behind.

ideas.title: Brain freeze isn't your brain freezing
ideas.angle: Explain the mechanism: cold hits the palate, the pain is referred to the forehead, and a small study saw an artery widen as the pain began and narrow as it faded.

ideas.title: Gulp vs sip: the brain freeze experiment
ideas.angle: Compare the two experiments: ice water gulped triggers brain freeze in half of people, an ice cube only in one in eight; fast ice cream doubles it in a school trial.

ideas.title: Why does cold in your mouth hurt your forehead?
ideas.angle: Pose the referred-pain puzzle, answer it, and connect it to migraine-prone people who get brain freeze more often.

ideas.title: Leap years aren't every four years
ideas.angle: Myth-bust the rule everyone learned: the year is 365.2422 days, every-4 leap days overshoot, the drift reached 10 days, and since 1582 century years only leap if they divide by 400.

ideas.title: The ten days that vanished in October 1582
ideas.angle: Tell the calendar's correction as a story: the Julian surplus piled up, Thursday 4 October was followed by Friday 15 October, and Britain skipped 11 days in 1752.

ideas.title: The three leap-year rules in one go
ideas.angle: A fast listicle: divide by 4 to leap, skip century years, but leap again if the year divides by 400, and why the third rule exists.

ideas.title: Was 2000 a leap year?
ideas.angle: A quiz built on the year most people get wrong, answered with the divide-by-400 rule.

ideas.title: A dead flamingo can still stand on one leg
ideas.angle: Myth-bust the 'hard balancing act': in the 2017 cadaver test the one-legged pose held with zero muscle, two legs did not, and live birds swayed less when they dozed.

ideas.title: Two reasons flamingos tuck a leg: warmth and effort
ideas.angle: Explain both supported explanations: more birds rest on one leg in water and in the cold (heat saving), and the pose costs almost no muscle (effort saving).

ideas.title: That backwards knee is an ankle
ideas.angle: Start from the anatomy most people get wrong (the visible joint is the ankle, the knee is hidden) and use it to show how the leg locks into a passive pillar.

ideas.title: One leg or two: which is harder for a flamingo?
ideas.angle: Run the comparison the lab ran: held upright, the body locked on one leg but could not be held stable on two, the opposite of what people expect.

ideas.title: The giant horizon Moon is not bigger
ideas.angle: Myth-bust what everyone has seen: same-settings photos show the same width, the low Moon is even about 1.5 percent farther away, and the size is added by the brain.

ideas.title: Shrink the giant Moon with a paper tube
ideas.angle: A tonight-you-can-try-it video: hold up a fingernail, then look through a paper tube, and watch the illusion collapse.

ideas.title: Why your brain inflates the horizon Moon
ideas.angle: Explain the leading idea: the brain treats the horizon Moon as farther away, so it scales it up; tested since Kaufman and Rock, still debated.

ideas.title: Camera versus eyes: who is right about the Moon?
ideas.angle: Put the camera and the eye side by side: the photo keeps the Moon the same width, the eye does not.
